et grundstof.explanation: "Et grundstof" means "a chemical element". It is built from "grund" (basic) and "et stof" (a substance). To name an element, say: "Ilt er et grundstof" (Oxygen is a chemical element).

et gudbarn.explanation: "Et gudbarn" means "a godchild". It is built from "gud" (god) and "et barn" (a child). The plural is "gudbørn", with "ø" in the second part. To say whose godchild someone is, say: "Hun er min søsters gudbarn" (She is my sister's godchild).

et guldbryllup.explanation: "Et guldbryllup" means "a golden wedding anniversary". It is built from "guld" (gold) and "et bryllup" (a wedding). The wedding day itself is "et bryllup": "Vi var til bryllup i lørdags" (We went to a wedding last Saturday).

et gulv.explanation: "Et gulv" means "a floor". To say something lies on the floor, say: "Bogen ligger på gulvet" (The book is on the floor). For a level of a building, use "en etage" (a story): "Vi bor på anden etage" (We live on the second floor).

et gulvtæppe.explanation: "Et gulvtæppe" means "a carpet". It is built from "et gulv" (a floor) and "et tæppe" (a blanket or rug). To say you vacuum it, say: "Jeg støvsuger gulvtæppet" (I vacuum the carpet).

et gymnasium.explanation: "Et gymnasium" means "a high school". In Denmark, it is a three-year school that prepares students for university. English speakers may think of a gym, but a gym for exercise is "et fitnesscenter" (a gym): "Jeg træner i et fitnesscenter" (I work out in a gym).

related.en: a primary and lower secondary school

et gys.explanation: "Et gys" means "a shudder". To say something gave you a shudder, say: "Det gav mig et gys" (It gave me a shudder).

et gæsteværelse.explanation: "Et gæsteværelse" means "a guest room". It is built from "en gæst" (a guest) and "et værelse" (a room). The part "gæste" also appears in "en gæstebog" (a guest book): "Skriv i gæstebogen" (Write in the guest book).

et gøremål.explanation: "Et gøremål" means "a chore". It comes from the verb "at gøre" (to do). To ask what is on the list for today, say: "Hvad er dagens gøremål?" (What are today's chores?)

gal.explanation: "Gal" means "crazy". It takes an "e" in the plural: "gale ideer" (crazy ideas). The form "galt" means "wrong", as in "Noget gik galt" (Something went wrong).

galskab.explanation: "En galskab" means "a crazy act". It comes from "gal" (crazy). To call something a crazy act, say: "Det er en galskab at gå uden jakke i dag" (It is a crazy act to go without a jacket today).

galt.explanation: "Galt" means "wrong", as in "Jeg gjorde noget galt" (I did something wrong). To say something is not bad, use "ikke galt" (not bad): "Det er ikke galt" (It is not bad). The word "gal" is different and means "crazy": "Er du gal?" (Are you crazy?)

gammel.explanation: "Gammel" means "old". To ask someone's age, say: "Hvor gammel er du?" (How old are you?) To give your age, say: "Jeg er tredive år gammel" (I am thirty years old).

gammeldags.explanation: "Gammeldags" means "old-fashioned". The opposite is "moderne" (modern). To say a kitchen is modern, say: "Vi har et moderne køkken" (We have a modern kitchen).

gang.explanation: "Gang" means "a time", as in one occasion. To say something happened twice, say: "to gange" (twice). To ask how many times, say: "Hvor mange gange?" (How many times?) The same word also means a hallway: "Skoene står i gangen" (The shoes are in the hallway). For time on the clock, use "tid" (time): "Jeg har ikke tid" (I do not have time).

ganske.explanation: "Ganske" means "quite". To show it is weaker than "meget" (very), compare: "ganske kold" (quite cold) is less cold than "meget kold" (very cold).

ganske vist.explanation: "Ganske vist" means "admittedly". To admit one point and then give the other side with "men" (but), say: "Det er ganske vist dyrt, men det er godt" (It is admittedly expensive, but it is good).

garanteret.explanation: "Garanteret" means "definitely". It comes from "en garanti" (a guarantee). To say you are sure someone will be late, say: "Han kommer garanteret for sent" (He is sure to be late).

gavepapir.explanation: "Gavepapir" means "wrapping paper". It is built from "en gave" (a gift) and "et papir" (a paper). To say you have run out of it, say: "Vi mangler gavepapir" (We are missing wrapping paper).

gavmild.explanation: "Gavmild" means "generous". To say what someone is generous with, put "med" (with) after it: "Hun er gavmild med sin tid" (She is generous with her time).

gavmildhed.explanation: "En gavmildhed" means "generosity". It comes from "gavmild" (generous). To say someone showed generosity, say: "Hun viste stor gavmildhed" (She showed great generosity).

gavn.explanation: "Gavn" means "benefit". To say you get use out of something, say: "Jeg har stor gavn af min cykel" (I get great use out of my bike). To say something helps children, say "til gavn for børn" (for the benefit of children): "Pengene går til gavn for børn" (The money goes to the benefit of children).

genbrug.explanation: "Genbrug" means "recycling". It is built from "gen" (again) and "brug" (use). The part "gen" also appears in "at genstarte" (to restart): "Prøv at genstarte routeren" (Try restarting the router). In Denmark, you take things to the recycling center, "en genbrugsstation": "Vi kører på genbrugsstationen" (We are driving to the recycling center).

generelt.explanation: "Generelt" means "in general". To say what is true overall but not today, say: "Generelt er bussen til tiden, men i dag var den sen" (In general the bus is on time, but today it was late). The word for "general" before a noun is "generel": "en generel regel" (a general rule).

genert.explanation: "Genert" means "shy". To say who you are shy around, use "over for" (towards): "Han er genert over for fremmede" (He is shy around strangers).
